entries.title: Mexico to try ‘El Chapo Isidro’ despite US extradition request
entries.summary: Fausto Meza Flores faces drug trafficking and weapons charges after his capture in a violent Sinaloa operation.
entries.content:
Fausto Meza Flores faces drug trafficking and weapons charges after his capture in a violent Sinaloa operation.

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro”, will be tried in Mexico despite an extradition request by the US, in a move that could worsen already-strained relations between the two countries.

Attorney General Ernestina Godoy told reporters on Monday that Mexican authorities “are going to put him on trial in this country”.

Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured after an hours-long firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen on Friday at a compound in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa. He was flown to Mexico City the following day.

He faces local charges for weapons offences and methamphetamine possession with intent to sell.

US involvement

Earlier on Monday, Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said Washington had requested Meza Flores’s extradition after his capture in the northern state of Sinaloa.

President Claudia Sheinbaum said US authorities provided intelligence support but did not participate directly on the ground.

US surveillance drones were authorised to help track Meza Flores before ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠the raid, authorities added, despite sensitivities over US anti-drug operations in the country in recent months.

Four Mexican soldiers and 16 alleged cartel gunmen were killed in the overnight operation, according to the Mexican Secretariat of National Defence.

Meza Flores is accused by US authorities of leading a major trafficking network that moved heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, marijuana and fentanyl across the border.

The US Department of Justice said he faces six charges in the US that include running a continuing criminal enterprise, narcoterrorism, money laundering conspiracy and weapons offences.

His arrest is the latest in a series of high-profile anti-cartel operations by Mexico, including the February killing of Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera, as US President Donald ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Trump presses ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌the Sheinbaum government to crack down on organised crime.

entries.title: UN chief calls for world to agree on AI oversight within a year
entries.summary: Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has become increasingly vocal about AI as end of term nears.
entries.content:
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has become increasingly vocal about AI as end of term nears.

United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has called for measures to better manage the risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) during a conference in Barbados.

“Today I call for member states to coordinate efforts and to develop within the next year a globally inclusive and principles-based multilateral framework for AI risk management, backed by independent and credible oversight,” Guterres said Monday.

Guterres, who is approaching the end of his term due in December, has become increasingly vocal about the need for safety measures around advanced technology to avoid a future in which “killer robots” are a reality.

‘Realities of today’s world’

Guterres said Monday at the Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety that “when one looks at different other institutions of global governance … they correspond to the reality of the world in 1945”.

“It’s clear that institutions need to be reformed in order to adapt themselves to the realities of today’s world,” he said.

“That applies to the UN, and that applies to the international financial architecture, that applies to the world trade system.”

Guterres said that he would advise his successor, due to take office in the new year but yet to be selected, that properly controlling AI would be necessary for “humanity to maintain control of our world”.

The AI race

International regulation of AI appears distant as the technology’s superpowers, the United States and China, continue to seek the upper hand in research and development breakthroughs.

Nonetheless, Guterres said that a starting point could be for countries to agree on shared safety measures, a testing regime and basic requirements for independent oversight.

In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX chief Elon Musk called for a slowdown in the development of AI.

Others, like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, want to move full steam ahead.

Regulators in the US, where AI development has proceeded at the fastest pace, appear unlikely to immediately intervene.

In September, US President Donald Trump hosted a group of American tech executives who agreed to abide by a voluntary code of conduct on AI safety.

entries.title: Appeals court renews Trump bid for federal jurisdiction in hush-money case
entries.summary: The ruling could clear the way for Trump to argue prosecutors relied on evidence protected by presidential immunity.
entries.content:
Monday’s ruling could clear the way for Trump to argue prosecutors relied on evidence protected by presidential immunity.

A federal appeals court has revived United States President Donald Trump’s bid to transfer his New York criminal hush-money case to federal court, months after a district judge rejected the effort for a third time.

On Monday, a three-judge panel of the 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals reversed a lower court ruling that had kept the case in New York state court.

In a two-page order, the 2nd Circuit panel said it disagreed with the late US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein’s denial of Trump’s request for the “removal” of his case to federal court.

The appeals court said Hellerstein had “erred in holding that removal is categorically unavailable in a state criminal case” after conviction.

It directed a federal judge in Manhattan to consider whether the proceedings could be brought under federal jurisdiction.

In a written statement provided to The Associated Press news agency, a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said the president “appreciates the 2nd Circuit’s prompt and correct ruling, as he continues to win against Democrat weaponization of our Justice System”.

Trump has sought to use presidential immunity in federal court to have his conviction overturned. He was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in 2024, though he has denied any wrongdoing.

Trump’s New York criminal conviction

The case stems from a $130,000 “hush money” payment made shortly before the 2016 presidential election to adult film performer Stormy Daniels.

Daniels had claimed she had an affair with the Republican leader while he was married — an allegation he denies — and prosecutors alleged that the money was intended to buy her silence during a tense campaign season.

Trump ultimately won the 2016 presidential election, ushering him into his first term in public office.

The payment was made through Trump’s former lawyer and fixer Michael Cohen. Prosecutors argued that Trump fudged his business records to pass off his reimbursements to Cohen as legal expenses, thereby concealing them from voters.

While falsifying business records is normally a misdemeanour offence, it can be charged as a felony if done in service of another crime. In Trump’s case, prosecutors said he violated state election laws.

In May 2024, a New York jury found him guilty, making Trump the first US president to be convicted of a crime.

At a sentencing hearing in January 2025 — shortly before his second term as president began — Trump received an unconditional discharge, meaning he faced neither imprisonment nor a financial penalty. But his conviction remains on the record.

Why does Trump want the case heard in federal court?

For years, Trump has sought to overturn that conviction.

Monday’s ruling leaves the jury’s guilty verdict intact, but it also clears the way for the president to seek a hearing in federal court.

He is expected to argue that state prosecutors secured his conviction by relying on evidence that would have been shielded by presidential immunity in federal court.

His legal team is likely to point to a landmark 2024 ruling as justification for that argument.

At the time, the Supreme Court’s conservative majority ruled that presidents could enjoy “presumptive immunity” for any “official acts” conducted while in office.

What constitutes an “official act”, however, is an open question. Previously, the Supreme Court had only conferred immunity to actions taken within a president’s constitutional authority.

Monday’s ruling reverses a series of setbacks for Trump’s legal team.

In August, federal judge Hellerstein rejected Trump’s third attempt to transfer the case, finding that the president’s arguments were insufficient to justify moving it out of state court.

Hellerstein, a senior federal judge in Manhattan’s Southern District of New York, died last month at the age of 92.

The move also stalls Trump’s state-level appeal in New York’s Appellate Division, which heard arguments earlier this month but has yet to rule on his challenge.

A federal judge has been directed to rule promptly on whether the case should indeed be transferred from New York state court to federal jurisdiction, although no deadline has been set.

entries.title: Israeli minister approves return of Flydubai flights to Tel Aviv
entries.summary: Final resumption of carrier's route between Dubai and Tel Aviv depends on Israeli security authorities' approval.
entries.content:
Final resumption of carrier’s route between Dubai and Tel Aviv depends on Israeli security authorities’ approval.

Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of Flydubai flights to Tel Aviv, according to Israeli media, almost two months after an onboard incident where a co-pilot was accused of attacking his captain.

Regev made the announcement on Monday, though Israel’s security authorities’ approval is still required for flights to resume. The ministry expects operations to resume within a week or two, Israeli media said.

The minister’s approval comes after talks between Israeli officials, led by ministry Director-General Moshe Ben-Zaken, and Emirati aviation officials took place in Dubai on November 16.

Authorities discussed potential security measures that would allow for airlines to fully resume flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv.

“The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident,” Israeli media reported, citing a transportation ministry statement. “As a result, Regev approved the return of Flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities.”

“The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers,” the statement added.

Flydubai halted flights to Tel Aviv on September 30 as it began an investigation into the events that transpired on board a Boeing 737 Max 8. Israeli carriers also stopped running routes to Dubai, making Etihad, which flies to Abu Dhabi, the only carrier flying between the UAE and Israel, according to Israeli media.

The co-pilot, who was identified as an Omani national, was arrested when the plane diverted and made an emergency landing in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the co-pilot of trying to crash the plane and of attacking the captain, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national.

The emergency came a day after Netanyahu warned of possible attacks in the lead-up to Israel’s October 27 parliamentary elections.

entries.title: Bukele shares details on deaths of Salvadoran troops in Haiti intervention
entries.summary: Bukele's military intervention in Haiti comes after four Salvadoran technicians were kidnapped by gangs in October.
entries.content:
Bukele’s military intervention in Haiti comes after four Salvadoran technicians were kidnapped by gangs in October.

Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele has identified the three soldiers from his Central American country who were killed while on an anti-gang mission in Haiti.

Late on Sunday, Bukele posted on social media that their names were Lieutenant Cristian Daniel Palacios Santos and Corporals Emerson Alexander Zepeda Zelada and Wilber Manuel Serrano Medina.

“Tragically, an accidental explosion during that mission claimed their lives,” Bukele said.

He also described instances in which the men had shown “bravery” in the past.

During “tests in El Salvador”, Bukele said that Zepeda Zelada and Serrano Medina took quick action to disarm a grenade lodged in a drone.

“It was not possible to steer the drone toward a completely safe area for it to crash,” Bukele said. “They were fully aware of the immense risk they were taking, yet they chose to act to protect others. And they succeeded.”

According to Bukele, Palacios Santos was admired for recently taking control during a “critical moment” in an operation in which some contractors allegedly retreated.

“He acted with speed and determination, managing to save several lives, including those of his own colleagues,” Bukele wrote. “We all applaud his bravery.”

He didn’t identify the contractors.

Bukele also used his post to pledge that Salvadoran troops who want to leave Haiti could do so immediately without facing reprisals.

Bukele makes a promise to Salvadorans

The Salvadoran soldiers killed last week were among 2,500 deployed to Haiti last month after four of their own went missing during an October 18 attack in gang-held territory. They have not yet been found.

Bukele said that his government would award the families of the three soldiers killed on Friday $200,000 in addition to a monthly income.

He also stressed that any soldier who wants to leave Haiti immediately may do so “without fear of reprisal and without concern that their return might jeopardise the mission, as many of their comrades have volunteered to relieve anyone who wishes to be relieved”.

Salvadoran troops have come under increased scrutiny as experts and the United Nations note they are operating in a largely unilateral way. Thousands of Haitians recently demonstrated to support Bukele.

The agreement between Haiti and El Salvador hasn’t been made public.

“There is no information on the scope and limits of its mission, nor on its accountability mechanisms,” according to a report published Monday by NAL Human Rights, a Netherlands-based consulting company focused on Central American issues.

It noted that, regardless of what that deal stipulates, Salvadoran and international laws require that El Salvador’s armed forces comply with human rights and humanitarian laws.

The report also underscored that the Central American country and the International Criminal Court have jurisdiction to prosecute Salvadoran military personnel if they are accused of war crimes, genocide or crimes against humanity.

More than 20,000 people have been killed in gang-related violence across Haiti in the past five years.

US lawmakers demand answers about the situation in Haiti

The deaths of the Salvadoran soldiers come as local and international forces fight powerful gangs entrenched in Martissant, a community located in a key corridor that links Haiti’s capital to the country’s western and southern regions.

Dozens of suspected gang members have been killed since last week as the battle in Martissant continues, police have said.

It is the first major operation in Martissant in the more than five years that gangs have controlled it.

As Haitian police and others continue to battle gangs in Martissant, a UN-backed gang suppression force said it killed several suspected gang members on Sunday as part of ongoing operations in Tabarre and Cite Soleil, located in Port-au-Prince, and in the northern town of Gros Morne.

As fighting intensifies, two Democratic lawmakers on Monday accused the administration of US President Donald Trump of failing to “name and sanction the political and economic elite fueling Haiti’s insecurity”.

The concern was outlined in a letter penned by New Hampshire Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and New York Representative Gregory Meeks, the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

“At a time when the Haitian people are preparing to vote for the first time in over a decade, Congress, the American public and the Haitian people deserve transparency about the nature and scale of collusion between gangs and their political and economic support networks,” they said.

The letter was addressed to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Haiti is scheduled to hold the first round of elections in July 2027. Among the candidates running are some previously sanctioned by the United States and Canada.

entries.title: US adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist after Nvidia spy scandal
entries.summary: Bureau of Security and Industry adds Singapore-based firm and six other entities to export control list.
entries.content:
Bureau of Security and Industry adds Singapore-based firm and six other entities to export control list.

The United States has added the Singapore-based company at the centre of an alleged spying scandal involving Nvidia to its trade blacklist.

The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) placed Megaspeed International and six other firms in Southeast Asia on its Entity List on Monday, hours after Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia as CEO in a stunning comeback that sent tech stocks soaring.

Megaspeed and the other entities were determined to be “acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States”, BIS, which sits under the US Department of Commerce, said in a filing to the Federal Register.

The designations mean that anyone seeking to ship the entities advanced US technology, including Nvidia’s top-end graphics processing units (GPUs) used in AI, must obtain an export licence.

Megaspeed’s blacklisting comes as divisions in US President Donald Trump’s administration over China’s access to Nvidia chips have been laid bare in recent weeks amid claims Huang was romantically involved with a woman accused of working with Chinese intelligence.

While US officials have been scrutinising Megaspeed’s compliance with export controls for years, US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s department had declined to place the company on its trade blacklist, prompting recriminations from administration officials known to hold more hawkish views on China, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Trump felt ‘very strongly’

Trump on Monday played down the national security concerns around Nvidia as he confirmed that he had personally intervened with the company’s board of directors to push for Huang’s reinstatement, telling CNBC he felt “very strongly” about the issue.

Shaoyu Yuan, a visiting assistant professor at New York University’s Center for Global Affairs who specialises in security issues, said Trump’s intervention was the latest example of the president making policy based on personal rapport rather than a “consistent security standard”.

“The incoherence is in the wider policy. Washington blacklists a middleman for moving Nvidia chips to China while it licenses Nvidia to sell H200 chips to China directly and takes a 25 percent cut,” Yuan told Al Jazeera, referring to the Trump administration’s announcement last year that it would allow the sale of some Nvidia GPUs to China in exchange for the chip giant handing over part of revenues to the government.

“Treasury Secretary Bessent has said other departments wanted this listing for months, and Commerce acted only after the scandal became public.”

US officials have accused Megaspeed International’s former top executive Alice Huang of working with China’s Ministry of State Security to target Huang in an intelligence-gathering operation.

Beijing has rejected the claims as “groundless speculation” and “an attempt to smear and malign China”.

Nvidia shares skyrocketed 31.5 percent following the news of Huang’s reinstatement, helping the US stock market achieve its strongest single-day performance in more than 18 months.

Concerns ‘serious, unresolved’

The six entities added to the trade blacklist along with Megaspeed International on Monday include three firms in Malaysia, two in Singapore and one in Thailand.

BIS named the entities as MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International, Speedmatrix, Apex Enterprise Solutions, Swiftdata and Megaspeed (Thailand).

Malaysia’s Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation, Singapore’s Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Thailand’s Ministry of Industry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the US Department of Justice on suspicion of diverting high-end chips to China in violation of export controls, did not respond to a request for comment.

The Singapore-based data centre company has previously insisted that it is a “legitimate and lawful business” and that media reports about its operations contained claims that were “not supported by verifiable evidence”.

Shiva Rajgopal, a professor of accounting at Columbia Business School, said it was “extraordinary” that the Trump administration had decided to blacklist Megaspeed while also pushing for Huang’s reinstatement.

“The board reinstated its CEO before the investigations into Megaspeed and his ties to it have concluded. Today’s listing shows those concerns are serious and unresolved,” Rajgopal told Al Jazeera.

“For the chip industry, the lesson is that knowing your customer is now a board-level issue,” Rajgopal said.

entries.title: What could Democrats do with their expanding congressional majority?
entries.summary: The Democratic Party is debating how best to use its large margin of victory in the US midterm elections.
entries.content:
The Democratic Party is debating how best to use its large margin of victory in the US midterm elections.

The Democratic Party has continued to expand its already sizeable majorities in the United States Congress as counting concludes in the final races of the 2026 midterm elections.

As of Monday, the Democrats hold a 258-seat majority in the 435-member House of Representatives. Four races remain uncalled.

All the races have been decided, meanwhile, for the Senate, where Democrats gained a 56-seat majority out of 100 total seats.

Flipping both chambers gives the party a strong hand to shape legislation during the last two years of Trump’s term in office.

How might the Democrats approach their role in government once the new Congress is sworn in on January 3? Find out in this quick explainer.

What do the results say?

The midterm results give Democrats their largest House majority since 1992 and their largest Senate majority in more than a decade. Republicans, meanwhile, saw their tally in the House drop to 173 seats, their lowest figure in years.

The vote also served as a firm rebuke of Trump’s second term as president, with voters venting their frustration over cost-of-living issues, the US-Israel war on Iran, aggressive immigration raids and corruption.

Democratic victories also extended well beyond traditional left-wing strongholds, with candidates racking up wins in Republican-led states such as Texas, Mississippi and South Carolina.

Which races remain?

Four House seats have yet to be called: one in Minnesota, one in Tennessee, and two in Louisiana that will be settled by a run-off on December 12.

Those races could see the Democrats further expand their majority in the House. The final count is now a question of just how large the party’s majority will be.

What will Democrats do with their majority?

Democrats have long pledged to use any congressional majorities they win as a check on Trump’s agenda.

But the scale of their success in the 2026 midterms has prompted discussion about embracing a more ambitious legislative agenda.

In the House of Representatives, Democrats have outlined a 100-day agenda that includes potentially reversing tax cuts that largely benefit wealthy earners and restoring healthcare subsidies that expired under Trump.

Lawmakers have also said that they will act to end the war on Iran, although divisions remain within the party over how to rein in Trump’s military actions. Under the US Constitution, Congress alone can authorise military operations.

Progressives have accused the party’s moderate wing of playing down expectations of firm steps to end the war, including cutting off funding.

Democrats have also pledged to use their newfound position to exercise oversight over the executive branch by launching probes and issuing subpoenas.

On Monday, for example, House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said that a Democrat-led Congress would conduct a “swift, thorough, and wide-ranging” investigation into the actions of the chip manufacturer Nvidia.

He also said it would delve into the “corrupt abuse of power” by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

In the Senate, Democrats have also threatened to block Trump’s nominees for high-level government positions, which require the chamber’s confirmation.

What role will Trump play?

While Democrats will hold substantial majorities in both chambers of Congress, Trump will retain the power to veto legislation.

Some lawmakers, however, have tried to persuade the president that he could benefit from working with Democrats after his party’s stark defeat in the midterms.

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, for example, has shared a series of tongue-in-cheek social media posts suggesting that a universal healthcare programme — a long-term progressive goal — could be named after the president in a bid to win his support.

“Donald, this is on the table,” El-Sayed said in a social media post showing a card for a hypothetical health insurance programme titled “Trumpcare”. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

Could Trump work with the Democrats?

There is little evidence, however, to suggest that Trump is planning a political pivot after the midterms.

Within a week of the vote, for instance, Trump named Stephen Miller — one of the architects of his hardline policies on immigration — as White House chief of staff.

The staffing shake-up was seen as a doubling-down on right-wing policy priorities.

While Trump has, at times, suggested that he could cooperate with Democratic lawmakers, he has also promised to use his veto power aggressively.

He has also taken to social media to disparage Chuck Schumer, who is currently seeking to become the next Senate majority leader, a position he previously held from 2021 to 2025.

“It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday.

“He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again.”

Trump’s White House has also threatened to take action if Democrats aggressively use their oversight powers in Congress.

“Members of the new Congress have evinced a clear intent to transgress” the constitutional limits of their power, White House counsel Will Scharf wrote in a letter on November 9, gesturing to the prospect of congressional investigations.
